description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Not an area we were particularly familiar with - apart from Fleet Street being associated, at one time, newspaper printing and the existing law courts / chambers. Lots of football fans on the train and even more, singing as they went, piled in to the tube entrance at Liverpool Street. With all that going on, we decided to walk. We stumbled upon surprise after surprise, all day. This being the first one - Christchurch Greyfriars Garden. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. Taken with my Fujifilm X-T30 II camera and a XF18-55mm lens. Velvia setting. London.

title: Monument to the great fire of London 1666.

description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

title: Paternoster Square Column. Central London.
description: The column is of Corinthian design made from Portland stone and topped with a gold leaf covered flaming copper urn, which is illuminated by fibre-optic lighting at night. The name comes from the medieval street on this site: Paternoster Row. After the Great Fire of London (1666) wiped out the the great multitude of shops here , the Stationer's returned, making it the heart of London's publishing trade before Fleet Street took the title. It survived until the second Great Fire of London: The Blitz (1940). The evening of 29th December 1940 was one of the most destructive air raids for London, and afterwards there were serious concerns that St Paul's cathedral would not survive on the adjacent site. In view of this the surrounding site was sacrificed and Paternoster Square was one of the casualties. The modern development owned by Mitsubishi Estate Co was designed by Whifield Partners in 1995. They chose to restore the medieval street plan of the area. The centrepiece of the square is the huge column similar the The Monument designed by Christopher Wren nearby to commemorate The Great fire of London. The flaming urn at the top of the Paternoster column is similar to Wren's design for The Monument and effectively commemorates both major fires in 1666 and 1940.

title: St. Vedast
tags: uk england london stvedast anglican church churches tower steeple
description: St. Vedast alias Foster. Founded in the 12th century by a Flemish community in London, the main part of the church was rebuilt between 1670 and 1673 on the old walls at a cost of £1,853, the least expensive of all Sir Christopher Wren's City commissions. The present tower was erected, possibly on its medieval lower stages, between 1695 and 1698. The three-tier spire, considered one of the most Baroque of all the City spires, was added between 1709 and 1712. The church was destroyed by bombing in December 1940 during the Blitz and was rebuilt from 1947 to 1953. Foster Lane.  The church is dedicated to a French saint known as Vedast, or Vedastus in Latin. He served as the Bishop of Arras in northern Gaul around the turn of the 6th century. Vedast played a crucial role in restoring the Christian Church in the region after it had suffered decades of destruction during the late Roman Empire due to invading tribes. He also worked to convert Clovis, the Frankish king.  DSC_0156

title: St. Paul's Cathedral
tags: uk england london church architecture cathedral stpauls churches christopherwren baroque anglican facade
description: St. Paul's Cathedral. Main Façade.  St. Paul's Cathedral was designed by Sir Christopher Wren and built between 1675 and 1710.  "The present church, designed by Sir Christopher Wren and begun in 1675, was opened for divine service on Dec. 2nd, 1697, and completed in 1710. The greater part of the cost of construction, which may be estimated at about 850,000£, was defrayed by a tax on coal entering the port of London. ... The façade, 180 ft. in breadth, presents a double portico, the lower part of which consists of 12 coupled Corinthian columns, 50 ft. high, and the upper of 8 Composite columns, 40 ft. high. On the apex of the pediment, which contains a relief of the Conversion of St. Paul, by Bird, rises a statue of St. Paul 15 ft. in height, with St. Peter and St. James on the right and left. On each side of the façade is a campanile tower, 222 ft . in height, with statues of the four Evangelists at the angles. The N. tower contains a fine peal of 12 bells, hung in 1878, and the other contains the largest bell in England ('Great Paul'), hung in 1882 and weighing more than 16 tons."--Baedeker 1915. title: Temple Bar Gate
description: Temple Bar Gate is an English Baroque arched gateway constructed between 1669 and 1672 over Fleet Street. It was dismantled in 1878 and rebuilt in 2002  as an entrance to Paternoster Square from St. Paul's Churchyard.  "... a gate-way formerly adjoining the Temple, between Fleet St. and the Strand, built by Wren in 1670. Its W. side was adorned with statues of Charles I and Charles II, its E. side with statues of Anne of Denmark and James I. The heads of criminals used to be barbarously exhibited on iron spikes on the top of the gate. The heavy wooden gates were afterwards removed to relieve the Bar of their weight, as it had shown signs of weakness; and the whole erection was taken down early in 1878, to permit of the widening of the street and to facilitate the enormous traffic. In 1888, the gate was re-erected near one of the entrances of Theobalds Park, Waltham Cross."--Baedeker 1915.  IMG_8718

title: The Duke of Wellington
tags: uk england london st pauls cathedral anglican church churches interior
description: St. Paul's Cathedral. Monument to Field Marshal Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington (1769-1852). Wellington died in 1852, but his monument was not completed until 1912 when the equestrian figure was unveiled.  "R., beneath the central arch of the aisle: Monument to the Duke of Wellington (d. 1852 ), by Alfred Stevens. The bronze figure of Wellington rests on a lofty sarcophagus, overshadowed by a rich marble canopy, with 12 Corinthian columns. Above are colossal groups of Valour and Cowardice, Truth and Falsehood. On the top is an equestrian statue of Wellington, modelled by Tweed from Stevens's sketches. This final completion of Stevens's design was placed in position in 1912."--Baedeker 1915.   IMG_8708

title: Lord Nelson
tags: uk england london st pauls cathedral anglican church churches interior crypt lordnelson tomb
description: St. Paul's Cathedral. Crypt. Tomo of Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson, 1st Duke of Bronte KB ( 1758-1805). Lord Nelson was killed in the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 and his coffin was made from the timber of a French ship he defeated in battle. The black marble sarcophagus that adorns his tomb was originally made for Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Chancellor, during Henry VIII's reign – until Wolsey fell from favour.  "Farther on, exactly under the centre of the dome, is the black marble sarcophagus of Nelson (d. 21st Oct., 1805), containing an inner coffin made of part of the mainmast of the French flag-ship L'Orient, which was blown up at Aboukir. The sarcophagus, the work of Benedetto da Rovezzano, was originally ordered by Card. Wolsey for himself."--Baedeker 1915.  IMG_8701

title: Quire Cieling
tags: uk england london st pauls cathedral anglican church churches interior quire choir mosaics
description: St. Paul's Cathedral. Quire (Choir). Sir William Blake Richmond created the mosaic ceiling in the Quire from 1891 to 1904. The three saucer domes depict The Creation of the Birds, The Creation of the Fishes, and The Creation of the Beasts. Richmond's The Risen Christ in Glory (Christ in Majesty) mosaic, created in 1893, is at the far end.  "The vaulting and walls of the choir are decorated in glass (smalto ) mosaic from designs by Sir W. B. Richmond, executed in the style of the early mosaicists, and not after the smooth modern method. The general effect adds largely to the richness and warmth of the choir ... On the central panel on the roof of the apse is Christ enthroned ...  The mosaics in the saucer-domes above the three bays in the choir proper represent (from E. to W.) the Creation of the Birds, of the Fishes, and of the Beasts."--Baedeker 1915.  DSC_0131p1

description: St. Paul's Cathedral. American Memorial Chapel. The apse and former Jesus Chapel were redesigned and dedicated in 1958 as the American Memorial Chapel. The chapel commemorates the 28,000 American service members stationed in the UK who died during World War II.  IMG_8684

title: Sacrifice Window
tags: uk england london st pauls cathedral anglican church churches interior brianthomas stainedglass window
description: St, Paul's Cathedral. Stained glass windows by Brian Thomas in the American Chapel (apse). The central window has the theme of "Sacrifice" and is dominated by an image of the Crucifixion. At the foot of the cross is the Virgin Mary, pierced by the sword of grief. Below the image of the Crucifixion are the images of the Ark – a ship in stormy waters, echoing both the ships that took the colonists to North America and the passage back across the Atlantic of hundreds of thousands of young men who were to take part in the liberation of Europe – and of a pelican. It stands One hundred and eleven metres tall and is a Church of England cathedral, the seat of the Bishop of London and Mother Church of the Diocese of London, It sits at the top of Ludgate Hill, the highest point in the City of London and was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1962   The first mention of a Christian building on this site was in 604, when a monastery was built here and dedicated to St. Paul. title: St Paul's Cathedral from hidden garden

description: One of London’s secret gardens had a major overhaul back in 2022 and Londoners are only just now finding out. The tiny park, next to 25 Cannon Street, features an oval reflection pool that perfectly frames an upside-down view of the dome of St Paul’s. It’s become a hotspot for London’s photographers, and those seeking a moment of quiet in the middle of the city. It’s stunningly picturesque, and a lovely little oasis, hidden in the middle of London  Foliage hides the minuscule park from the street, and in turn, hides the city from the park. You won’t really see it from the outside, and from the inside, you’ll all but forget you’re in London.  St Paul's cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for over 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

title: St Paul's Cathedral, London
tags: england london stpauls cathedral church history historic architecture city building sky clouds sirchristopherwren ludatehill baroque dome anglican nikon d60 captureone
description: One of my favorite sites in London, and one of the most beautiful cathedrals I've ever seen, St Paul's is easy to get to and a joy to visit. Don't miss the crypt below, which is fully renovated and ironically features a convenient cafe. So many British greats are entombed here, too many to relate, but Horatio Nelson and the Duke of Wellington are must-sees. If you can make the climb to the top, the Whispering Gallery and Dome exterior are well-worth the effort. From Wikipedia: St Paul's Cathedral is an Anglican cathedral, the seat of the Bishop of London and the mother church of the Diocese of London. It sits on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication to Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. The present church, dating from the late 17th century, was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. Its construction, completed in Wren's lifetime, was part of a major rebuilding programme in the City after the Great Fire of London. The cathedral is one of the most famous and most recognisable sights of London. Its dome, framed by the spires of Wren's City churches, dominated the skyline for 300 years. At 365 feet (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1962. The dome is among the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second largest church building in area in the United Kingdom after Liverpool Cathedral. St Paul's Cathedral occupies a significant place in the national identity. It is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz. Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington and Sir Winston Churchill; Jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer, the launch of the Festival of Britain and the thanksgiving services for the Golden Jubilee, the 80th Birthday and the Diamond Jubilee of Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. *Press L for best viewing. Link to ~My best photos~ *** All my photos are © All Rights Reserved. ***

title: East London Bus and Coach Company Limited (T/A Stagecoach London) Alexander Dennis Enviro 400MMC Hybrid
description: A significant vehicle  This bus is a significant vehicle in the history of London’s Buses. On July 7 2005 a suicide bomber detonated a bomb on a Stagecoach London TransBus Trident/TransBus ALX400 in Tavistock Square.killing himself and thirteen others. The bus itself was on diversion because of three earlier bonbs set off on the Underground. Indeed it’s believed that the bomber only got on the bus because he couldn’t get on the Underground. In total some 200 people were victims of the attacks.   To replace the Trident, Stagecoach London received the very first Enviro 400 with markings honouring the victims. With that earlier bus being withdrawn and into preservation, this is the new vehicle to mark that dreadful day, 11377 (SK20BBF).

title: National Firefighters Memorial, Sermon Lane, London
description: The bronze memorial, sculpted by John W Mills, depicts three firefighters in action during the Blitz. It was originally intended as a tribute to the firefighters who lost their lives in the Blitz and in World War II, and was unveiled by the Queen Mother in May 1991. In 1998 it was decided to extend it to be a tribute to all UK firefighters who were killed in the line of duty. It was rededicated in September 2003 by the Princess Royal.

Photograph taken at an altitude of Twenty six metres at 12:53pm on Friday 23rd February 2024 off St Paul's Churchyard and Queens Head Passage, of one of the two old wooden tool gates which were completed in 1672 for the Temple Bar gateway in the City of Westminster, London.   The original 14th century wooden toll gates were located on Fleet Street and survived the Great Fire of London, but a new stone building saw the need for these newer gates. The stone structure and these gates were bought for £1 in 1984 by the Temple Bar trust who then spent £3 million rebuilding the archway and gates as we know them today, completed in November 2005.       Once called Paternoster Row, this area was once the centre of the London publishing trade and destroyed by aerial bombardment during the Second World War Blitz. It is now the location for the London Stock Exchange and now features the re-erected 1669 Temple Bar Gate by Christopher Wren which was restored and placed here in 2004 at a cost of three million pounds.   The Paternoster Square Column is a Corinthian column of Portland stone with gold leaf covered flaming copper urn that is illuminated by fibre optic lights at night. title: St Vedast, London
tags: viltroxaf20mmf28z london church sirchristopherwren nikonz7
description: 1670-73 by Wren. Tower 1697. Interior burnt in World War II and rebuilt in near facsimile. Rectangular body with south aisle and clerestory. Integral south-west tower. Plain west front of Portland stone with central doorway, 2 arched windows above and central opening with mullions and transoms. Parapet to roof which is repeated on south side where main wall is of rubble or red brick. East elevation rendered, with 3 arched windows and circular opening in central attic. Portland stone tower with arched and circular openings and particularly fine stone steeple.  The three-tier spire is considered one of the most baroque of all the City spires, was added in 1709–12 at a cost of £2,958. With this completion date, it is thought to be the last of Wren's city churches to be finished.

title: St Paul’s Cathedral, London
tags: viltroxaf20mmf28z london cathedral stpaulscathedral sirchristopherwren nikonz7
description: By Sir Christopher Wren, 1675 to 1710. Rebuilding of medieval cathedral burnt in Great Fire. Classical style, mainly of Portland stone, with central dome and western towers. Large crypt. Contains important contemporary and later fittings and monuments including a very few survivals from the previous church. C19 fittings, monuments, decorations etc of importance. Dome painted by Thornhill. Above the two west chapels are the library and music room. The south west tower contains a fine circular staircase. Elaborate steps with walls, piers, urns and gates to south transept. Broad steps to west front flanked by pedestals supporting decorative iron lamp standards by Lutyens.  Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria and the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer.

description: La cattedrale di San Paolo (in inglese St Paul's Cathedral o anche solo St Paul's) è una delle due cattedrali anglicane di Londra (l'altra è quella di Southwark), in Ludgate Hill, nella City. Chiesa madre della diocesi anglicana di Londra, l'imponente edificio è considerato il capolavoro dell'architetto Christopher Wren. È il primo edificio religioso per dimensione in Gran Bretagna.  Edifici religiosi che richiamano lo stile classico come questo in Inghilterra sono arrivati precedentemente solo con Inigo Jones che agli inizi del XVII secolo, in un ambiente nordico legato allo stile gotico, importò il classicismo italiano, completando il panorama architettonico del rinascimento inglese.  Tra gli eventi più famosi che qui hanno avuto luogo si ricordano il funerale dell'ammiraglio Nelson, quello del duca di Wellington, quello di Sir Winston Churchill e quello di Margaret Thatcher; le celebrazioni giubilari della regina Vittoria; i te deum per la fine della prima e della seconda guerra mondiale; il matrimonio tra il principe Carlo e la principessa Diana; il pranzo del Festival of Britain; i festeggiamenti per i giubilei della regina Elisabetta II (argento, oro, diamanti e 80º e 90º compleanno della regina).

title: The Dome of St Paul's Cathedral
tags: dome england stpaul’scathedral london unitedkingdom
description: St Paul’s Cathedral designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for over 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Wren drew inspiration from Michelangelo's dome of St Peter's Basilica, and that of Mansart's Church of the Val-de-Grâce, which he had visited. Unlike those of St Peter's and Val-de-Grâce, the dome of St Paul's rises in two clearly defined storeys of masonry, which, together with a lower unadorned footing, equal a height of about 95 feet. From the time of the Greek Cross Design it is clear that Wren favoured a continuous colonnade (peristyle) around the drum of the dome, rather than the arrangement of alternating windows and projecting columns that Michelangelo had used and which had also been employed by Mansart. Summerson suggests that he was influenced by Bramante's "Tempietto" in the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio. In the finished structure, Wren creates a diversity and appearance of strength by placing niches between the columns in every fourth opening. The peristyle serves to buttress both the inner dome and the brick cone which rises internally to support the lantern. Above the peristyle rises the second stage surrounded by a balustraded balcony called the "Stone Gallery". This attic stage is ornamented with alternating pilasters and rectangular windows which are set just below the cornice, creating a sense of lightness. Above this attic rises the dome, covered with lead, and ribbed in accordance with the spacing of the pilasters. It is pierced by eight light wells just below the lantern, but these are barely visible. They allow light to penetrate through openings in the brick cone, which illuminates the interior apex of this shell, partly visible from within the cathedral through the ocular opening of the lower dome. The lantern, like the visible masonry of the dome, rises in stages. The most unusual characteristic of this structure is that it is of square plan, rather than circular or octagonal. The tallest stage takes the form of a tempietto with four columned porticos facing the cardinal points. Its lowest level is surrounded by the "Golden Gallery" and its upper level supports a small dome from which rises a cross on a golden ball. The total weight of the lantern is about 850 tons.

title: St Paul's Cathedral
tags: panasonics5ii highresolutionmode hhhr handheldnightshot 100xthe2024edition 100x2024 image6100 silkypixdeveloperstudiopro10
description: From the St Paul's website:  "St Paul’s has a long tradition of honouring and welcoming champions of equality and social justice – from the prison reformer John Howard, who was the first ‘civilian’ to be given a statue on the Cathedral floor, to Martin Luther King, who preached a sermon to thousands of worshippers in 1964.  In 1958, the actor and singer Paul Robeson became the first Black person to read The Lesson in the Cathedral. Robeson was invited by John Collins, a Canon of the Cathedral, to sing at Evensong on the 12th October 1958. Robeson’s appearance raised funds for the Defence in the South African Treason Trials, in which 156 people, including Nelson Mandela, were accused of treason. The service was attended by so many, that many people stood, and huge crowds spilled outside onto the Cathedral steps. On a visit to South Africa in 1954, Collins was horrified by the racial segregation and oppression that he witnessed. In response to the apartheid government’s increasingly repressive regime, he established the Defence and Aid Fund to pay activists’ legal expenses and care for their families.   Working closely with his wife Diana, who wrote much of the early campaign literature, Collins initiative soon became an international network. From his office in the Cathedral precinct, millions of pounds in legal aid was secretly channelled to activists including Nelson Mandela and Walter Sisulu. His work in this field was recognized in 1978 by the award of the gold medal of the United Nations Special Committee Against Apartheid."  100x: The 2024 Edition  6/100 London landmarks by night

title: Stagecoach London LT266 - LTZ 1266
tags: stagecoach london tfl bow bw lt266 wright new routemaster ltz1266 ltz 1266
description: Ah, the City under the dusk. And New Routemasters, thankfully, aren't that much in vogue in the heart of it. Lest we ignore the 8 to Tottenham Court Road, of course. I remember photographing the other side of it back in 2019 on some far off side of Westminster or... wherever I was, and, well, here's the other end of it, sitting here presumably awaiting a next run on the route. Ah, Bow. What an interesting fleet you have.  Stagecoach London's LT266, a 2016 Wright New Routemaster based at Bow garage (BW), is seen here waiting time along Cheapside - much the subject of poetry from English modules I was actively studying at the time - on route 8 to Tottenham Court Road.

title: Stagecoach London 11397 - SK20 BDV
tags: stagecoach london tfl bow bw 11397 adl enviro400 mmc enviro 400mmc sk20bdv sk20 bdv
description: There they are! I was wondering where these would show up! And thankfully, most, if not all of them that I encountered this weekend still all had their old Stagecoach logos on them. I suspect vehicles from this batch to be among the last vehicles delivered to Stagecoach with the old 'Beachball' interior - across the country, the Local livery was just getting underway, with buses already delivered with the new interior in Oxfordshire, Greater Manchester and the North East, but oddly enough, it would seem London had to cling on with the old 'Beachball' style. Possibly down to the fact the new interiors depended on leather seating, which Stagecoach might not have been able to spec for London at the time. Of course, now, the Future Bus project is underway, meaning London is getting some leather-seated buses, so might this be privy to change? Finally the first of the 20-plates within the City, Stagecoach London's 11397, a 2020 ADL Enviro400 MMC based at Bow garage (BW), is seen down the A40 on route 25 to City Thameslink.

title: Stagecoach London 12537 - SN66 WSE
tags: stagecoach london tfl ash grove hk 12537 adl enviro400 city enviro 400 e400 sn66wse sn66 wse exhct 2537
description: While getting in the usual beauty shots of St Pauls Cathedral in, unfortunately just missing the National Firefighters Memorial by the looks of it, there was also an opportunity to catch a photo of yet another ex-CT Plus E400 City - which turned out to be the penultimate one of the whole trip, despite constantly seeing them throughout the weekend. Why? The old 'boycott because you've seen too many' mistake. Ah well. Hey, at least I caught the 'Walkie Talkie' in the background, though!  The penultimate photograph of one of these buses of the day, Stagecoach London's 12537, a 2016 ADL Enviro400H City new to CT Plus London as their 2537 and currently based at Stagecoach's Ash Grove garage (HK), passes by St Paul's Cathedral on Cannon Street as it works a 26 to Waterloo Station.

title: Bridgits Bakery 'Paddington Afternoon Tea Bus Tour' RM776 - 776 DYE
tags: bridgits bakery afternoon tea tour rm776 park royal aec routemaster 776dye 776 dye exlondon
description: Finally, St. Paul's Cathedral! And almost as soon as I'd reached it, I'm greated by the sight of a Routemaster. Although maybe I shouldn't have jinxed myself by repeatedly saying I had no relative interest in the type, because trying to photograph this - and any other RMs in London - proved fairly difficult. Settle for this photograph of it at the traffic lights instead. Interestingly enough, just as I came up and attempted to photograph this, I spied another photographer doing the same. I wonder if they have posted that photo somewhere?  Seen just in front of St. Paul's Cathedral at the traffic lights is Bridgits Bakery 'Paddington Afternoon Tea Tour'-branded RM776, a 1963 Park Royal-bodied AEC Routemaster that was, until 2014, used on Heritage Route 9.

title: A brand new DMS1681 (GM) seen in the Lord Mayor's Show of 1974
tags: london fleetline lordmayorsshow dms dms1681
description: A shot taken by me after climbing a roadside tree (aged 12!) - one of the brand new DMS 'Londoners' representing London Transport - seen in the Lord Mayor's Show cavalcade. Here's a history of DMS1681 - taken from 'Ian's Bus Stop': www.countrybus.org/DMS/DMSa16.htm DMS1681 (THM 681M) 10/74 new to Aldenham: 2/2DM4/1: MCCW/Leyland O.680 1974 used in Lord Mayor's Show AW (Abbey Wood) 12/77 AW repaint 78-80 AW 1/81 PR transfer (Poplar) 7/81 PR withdrawn into store sold to Ensign Bus (Purfleet) adopted for PSV service, Ensignbus 4/84 bought by Youngs, Rampton, for spares 6/85 Youngs, Rampton: spares So the bus only lasted seven years in LT service. Taken with my basic Kodak Brownie using 120 roll film. You can see a random selection of my bus photographs here on Flickriver: www.flickriver.com/photos/southallroutemaster/random/

description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Not an area we were particularly familiar with - apart from Fleet Street being associated, at one time, newspaper printing and the existing law courts / chambers. Lots of football fans on the train and even more, singing as they went, piled in to the tube entrance at Liverpool Street. With all that going on, we decided to walk. We stumbled upon surprise after surprise, all day. This being the first one - Christchurch Greyfriars Garden. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. Taken with my Fujifilm X-T30 II camera and a XF18-55mm lens. Velvia setting. London.

description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

description: St. Paul's Cathedral London, England, U.K. 03-20-25 The main entrance to St. Paul's, an Anglican Cathedral built in 1710. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honor of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. The statue is an 1886 copy of the original statue from 1712 by Francis Bird of Queen Anne, who was the British monarch when the Cathedral was completed. The image was shot with my extreme wide angle lens at 10mm. I haven't added too much lens correction, and I digitally erased over 45 people in this shot! The location of "The City of London" dates to the early Roman settlement of "Londinium" in AD 43. From Wikipedia: The City of London, also known as the City, is a ceremonial county and local government district with city status in England. It forms financial nucleus and historic center of London, however it forms only a small part of the larger Greater London metropolis. It forms part of the administrative area of Greater London, but not the ceremonial county. The boundries of "The City" are marked with 14 "watchdragon" figures along the roads and the River Thames. description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Not an area we were particularly familiar with - apart from Fleet Street being associated, at one time, newspaper printing and the existing law courts / chambers. Lots of football fans on the train and even more, singing as they went, piled in to the tube entrance at Liverpool Street. With all that going on, we decided to walk. We stumbled upon surprise after surprise, all day. This being the first one - Christchurch Greyfriars Garden. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

description: St. Paul's Cathedral London, England, U.K. 03-20-25 The main entrance to St. Paul's, an Anglican Cathedral built in 1710. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honor of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. The statue is an 1886 copy of the original statue from 1712 by Francis Bird of Queen Anne, who was the British monarch when the Cathedral was completed. The image was shot with my extreme wide angle lens at 10mm. I haven't added too much lens correction, and I digitally erased over 45 people in this shot! The location of "The City of London" dates to the early Roman settlement of "Londinium" in AD 43. From Wikipedia: The City of London, also known as the City, is a ceremonial county and local government district with city status in England. It forms financial nucleus and historic center of London, however it forms only a small part of the larger Greater London metropolis. It forms part of the administrative area of Greater London, but not the ceremonial county. The boundries of "The City" are marked with 14 "watchdragon" figures along the roads and the River Thames. description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross. description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

title: Christchurch Greyfriars Garden.
tags: 2025 christchurchgreyfriars cityoflondon ec1 england fujixt30ii fujifilmxt30ii garden london uk unitedkingdom xf1855mm church flowers velviasetting
description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Not an area we were particularly familiar with - apart from Fleet Street being associated, at one time, newspaper printing and the existing law courts / chambers. Lots of football fans on the train and even more, singing as they went, piled in to the tube entrance at Liverpool Street. With all that going on, we decided to walk. We stumbled upon surprise after surprise, all day. This being the first one - Christchurch Greyfriars Garden. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. Taken with my Fujifilm X-T30 II camera and a XF18-55mm lens. Velvia setting. London.

title: Monument to the great fire of London 1666.

description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

title: St Pauls cathedral  London.
tags: london tourist travel cityoflondon citytour history canon cityscapt streets londoncity citybreak buildings architecture cathedral england stpauls dome eos1100d
description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

Its dedication in honor of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral   St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

title: Paternoster Square Column. Central London.
description: The column is of Corinthian design made from Portland stone and topped with a gold leaf covered flaming copper urn, which is illuminated by fibre-optic lighting at night. The name comes from the medieval street on this site: Paternoster Row. After the Great Fire of London (1666) wiped out the the great multitude of shops here , the Stationer's returned, making it the heart of London's publishing trade before Fleet Street took the title. It survived until the second Great Fire of London: The Blitz (1940). The evening of 29th December 1940 was one of the most destructive air raids for London, and afterwards there were serious concerns that St Paul's cathedral would not survive on the adjacent site. In view of this the surrounding site was sacrificed and Paternoster Square was one of the casualties. The modern development owned by Mitsubishi Estate Co was designed by Whifield Partners in 1995. They chose to restore the medieval street plan of the area. The centrepiece of the square is the huge column similar the The Monument designed by Christopher Wren nearby to commemorate The Great fire of London. The flaming urn at the top of the Paternoster column is similar to Wren's design for The Monument and effectively commemorates both major fires in 1666 and 1940.

description: With the weather looking reasonable on the Sunday before the Bank Holiday, my better half and I got the train to London. We fancied a bit of an explore around Fleet Street / High Holborn. Not an area we were particularly familiar with - apart from Fleet Street being associated, at one time, newspaper printing and the existing law courts / chambers. Lots of football fans on the train and even more, singing as they went, piled in to the tube entrance at Liverpool Street. With all that going on, we decided to walk. We stumbled upon surprise after surprise, all day. This being the first one - Christchurch Greyfriars Garden. Seems the garden was laid out, to repeat the lines of the Wren church that once stood here. The body of the church saw some war action in 1940, so now only the west tower remains. description: Monument to the Great Fire of London  The Monument to the Great Fire of London, more commonly known simply as the Monument, is a fluted Doric column in London, England, situated near the northern end of London Bridge. Commemorating the Great Fire of London, it stands at the junction of Monument Street and Fish Street Hill, 202 feet (61.6 m) in height and 202 feet west of the spot in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. Constructed between 1671 and 1677, it was built on the site of St Margaret, New Fish Street, the first church to be destroyed by the Great Fire. It is Grade I-listed and is a scheduled monument.[3] Another monument, the Golden Boy of Pye Corner, marks the point near Smithfield where the fire was stopped.  Description  Viewing platform at the top of the Monument The Monument comprises a Doric column built of Portland stone topped with a gilded urn of fire. It was designed by Robert Hooke.[2] Its height marks its distance from the site of the shop of Thomas Farriner (or Farynor), the king's baker, where the blaze began.[4]

description: St Paul's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of St Paul the Apostle, is an Anglican cathedral in London, England, the seat of the Bishop of London. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London in the Church of England. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honour of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604.[4] The high-domed present structure, which was completed in 1710, is a Grade I listed building that was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. The cathedral's reconstruction was part of a major rebuilding programme initiated in the aftermath of the Great Fire of London.[5] The earlier Gothic cathedral (Old St Paul's Cathedral), largely destroyed in the Great Fire, was a central focus for medieval and early modern London, including Paul's walk and St Paul's Churchyard, being the site of St Paul's Cross.  The cathedral is one of the most famous and recognisable sights of London. Its dome, surrounded by the spires of Wren's City churches, has dominated the skyline for more than 300 years. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963. The dome is still one of the highest in the world. St Paul's is the second-largest church building in area in the United Kingdom, after Liverpool Cathedral.  Services held at St Paul's have included the funerals of Admiral Lord Nelson, the Duke of Wellington, Winston Churchill and Margaret Thatcher; jubilee celebrations for Queen Victoria; an inauguration service for the Metropolitan Hospital Sunday Fund;[6] peace services marking the end of the First and Second World Wars; the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer; the launch of the Festival of Britain; and the thanksgiving services for the Silver, Golden, Diamond, and Platinum Jubilees and the 80th and 90th birthdays of Queen Elizabeth II. St Paul's Cathedral is the central subject of much promotional material, as well as of images of the dome surrounded by the smoke and fire of the Blitz.[7] The cathedral is a working church with hourly prayer and daily services. The tourist entry fee at the door is £25 for adults (January 2024) but no charges are made to worshippers attending services, or for private prayer.[8]  The nearest London Underground station is St Paul's, which is 130 yards (120 m) away from St Paul's Cathedral.[9]  History Before the cathedral The location of Londinium's original cathedral is unknown, but legend and medieval tradition claim it was St Peter upon Cornhill. St Paul is an unusual attribution for a cathedral and suggests there was another one in the Roman period. Legends of St Lucius link St Peter upon Cornhill as the centre of the Roman Londinium Christian community. It stands upon the highest point in the area of old Londinium, and it was given pre-eminence in medieval procession on account of the legends. There is, however, no other reliable evidence, and the location of the site on the Forum makes it difficult for it to fit the legendary stories. In 1995, a large fifth-century building on Tower Hill was excavated and has been claimed as a Roman basilica, possibly a cathedral, although this is speculative.[10][11]  The Elizabethan antiquarian William Camden argued that a temple to the goddess Diana had stood during Roman times on the site occupied by the medieval St Paul's Cathedral.[12] Wren reported that he had found no trace of any such temple during the works to build the new cathedral after the Great Fire, and Camden's hypothesis is no longer accepted by modern archaeologists.[13]

description: St. Paul's Cathedral London, England, U.K. 03-20-25 The main entrance to St. Paul's, an Anglican Cathedral built in 1710. The cathedral serves as the mother church of the Diocese of London. It is on Ludgate Hill at the highest point of the City of London. Its dedication in honor of Paul the Apostle dates back to the original church on this site, founded in AD 604. The statue is an 1886 copy of the original statue from 1712 by Francis Bird of Queen Anne, who was the British monarch when the Cathedral was completed. The image was shot with my extreme wide angle lens at 10mm. I haven't added too much lens correction, and I digitally erased over 45 people in this shot! The location of "The City of London" dates to the early Roman settlement of "Londinium" in AD 43. From Wikipedia: The City of London, also known as the City, is a ceremonial county and local government district with city status in England. It forms financial nucleus and historic center of London, however it forms only a small part of the larger Greater London metropolis. It forms part of the administrative area of Greater London, but not the ceremonial county. The boundries of "The City" are marked with 14 "watchdragon" figures along the roads and the River Thames.
